cases.title: Pendakwa Raya v Mohd Riedzuan bin Hamzah
cases.court: High Court of Malaya (criminal jurisdiction) — listed on eJudgment as "Mahkamah Tinggi"
cases.outcome: The accused pleaded guilty to alternative possession charges after the original trafficking charges were reduced, and was sentenced to 8 years' imprisonment per charge running from the date of arrest, the terms to run concurrently, together with the statutory minimum of 10 strokes of whipping per charge (20 strokes cumulatively).
cases.summary: The accused originally faced charges of trafficking in dangerous drugs under s 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952. The charges were reduced to alternative possession charges under s 12(2), punishable under s 39A(2), involving 16.3g of heroin and monoacetylmorphines and 56.4g of methamphetamine, to which he pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity. In its sentencing grounds the High Court weighed public interest and deterrence against rehabilitation, applied the principle of proportionality, and emphasised that an accused must be sentenced for the offence he is actually convicted of and not for the original, more serious trafficking allegation. The court noted that the drug weights were only marginally above the presumption thresholds in s 37(da), and took into account the early guilty plea, the accused's status as a first offender, his personal circumstances and the prevailing sentencing trend. It imposed 8 years' imprisonment on each charge, backdated to the date of arrest under s 282(d) of the Criminal Procedure Code, ordered the terms to run concurrently applying the one-transaction rule and the totality principle (ss 288(5) and 289 CPC), and imposed the statutory minimum 10 strokes of whipping on each charge, totalling 20 strokes.
cases.keyPoint: An accused who pleads guilty to a reduced charge must be sentenced for the offence of conviction, not for the original and graver charge, with the totality and one-transaction principles governing whether multiple terms run concurrently.
cases.plain: A man was first accused of drug trafficking, which can carry the heaviest penalties. The prosecution agreed to lower the charges to simple drug possession, and he admitted guilt straight away. The judge said it would be wrong to punish him as if he were still a trafficker — he had to be punished for what he actually admitted to. Taking into account his early admission, his clean record and his personal situation, but also the public interest in deterring drug crime, the judge gave him 8 years in prison on each charge, counted from the day he was arrested, with the sentences served at the same time rather than one after the other, plus the minimum caning the law requires.

cases.title: Pendakwa Raya v Zulhaffiz bin Zulkifli
cases.court: High Court of Malaya (criminal jurisdiction) — listed on eJudgment as "Mahkamah Tinggi"
cases.outcome: The grounds concern sentencing for possession of 958.8g of cannabis after the trafficking charge was reduced to possession under s 6 punishable under s 39A(2), and address whether a sentence of 8 years' imprisonment and 10 strokes of whipping was adequate. The published catchwords record the issues rather than stating the final order in terms, so the precise disposal is not reproduced here.
cases.summary: The accused was originally charged with trafficking in 958.8g of cannabis under s 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952. That charge was reduced to possession under s 6, punishable under s 39A(2), and he pleaded guilty to the alternative charge. The published catchwords record a prosecution appeal against sentence and frame the central question as whether 8 years' imprisonment and 10 strokes of whipping were adequate. The court's reasoning treats the sheer quantity of cannabis as the principal aggravating factor, noting that the weight exceeded the presumption threshold in s 37(da)(vi), and also records the accused's attempt to flee arrest. Against that, the grounds record unchallenged mitigating factors: a guilty plea at the earliest opportunity, first-offender status, hardship to his family, and evidence of remorse and self-reform while in detention. The court set these considerations against the sentencing trend for comparable offences and the familiar tension between public interest and deterrence on one side and rehabilitation on the other, with whipping governed by s 289 and the commencement of the sentence from the date of arrest under s 282(d) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
cases.keyPoint: In drug possession sentencing, the quantity involved is the dominant aggravating factor, but it must still be balanced against an early guilty plea, first-offender status and genuine evidence of reform.
cases.plain: A man caught with just under a kilogram of cannabis was first accused of trafficking, but the charge was lowered to possession and he admitted it immediately. The question before the judge was whether 8 years in prison and 10 strokes of the cane was a fair punishment. The judge explained that the large amount of drugs was the most serious feature of the case, and that the man had also tried to run away when arrested. On the other hand, he owned up at once, had never been in trouble before, his family was suffering, and he had shown real signs of changing while locked up. The judge weighed all of this against what other courts have handed down in similar cases.

cases.title: Mohd Adli bin Jusoh v Pendakwa Raya
cases.court: High Court of Malaya (criminal appellate jurisdiction) — listed on eJudgment as "Mahkamah Tinggi"
cases.coram: YA Tuan Mohd Rosli bin Yusoff
cases.outcome: An appeal to the High Court against the whole of the Sessions Court's decision convicting and sentencing the appellant under s 14(d) of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017. The published catchwords set out the grounds argued rather than expressly recording the final order, so the disposal is not reproduced here.
cases.summary: The appellant was tried to a full trial in the Sessions Court and convicted under s 14(d) of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017, an offence carrying imprisonment of up to twenty years and liability to whipping. He appealed to the High Court against the whole of the Sessions Court judge's decision — both conviction and sentence. As recorded in the eJudgment catchwords, two issues were raised: first, whether the Sessions Court judge erred in law in holding that the prosecution had made out a prima facie case at the close of its case, which would have required the appellant to enter his defence; and second, whether the judge erred in fact and in law in passing sentence without giving full weight to the mitigating factors advanced on the appellant's behalf. The judgment therefore engages the standard appellate questions in child sexual offence prosecutions: the correctness of the prima facie finding on the evidence led, and whether the sentence reflected a proper balance between the gravity of an offence against a child and the personal mitigation of the accused.
cases.keyPoint: On a criminal appeal the High Court reviews both whether a prima facie case was properly found at the close of the prosecution case and whether the sentencing court gave due weight to mitigating circumstances.
cases.plain: A man was found guilty in the Sessions Court, after a full trial, of a sexual offence against a child and was sentenced. He appealed to the higher court, arguing two things: that the trial judge should never have required him to put on a defence because the prosecution's evidence was not strong enough, and that when the judge sentenced him she did not properly take into account the personal factors that should have reduced the punishment. The High Court's written reasons deal with both of those complaints.

cases.title: Dato' Seri Timor Shah Rafiq v Nautilus Tug & Towage Sdn. Bhd.
cases.court: High Court of Malaya at Kuala Lumpur (Mahkamah Tinggi) — Commercial Division (NCC)
cases.coram: YA Puan Elaine Yap Chin Gaik
cases.dateRaw: 12 October 2026 (grounds of judgment uploaded to the e-Judgment portal on 13 November 2026)
cases.outcome: The defendant's application to set aside the earlier, already-perfected order granting leave to commence a statutory derivative action was dismissed.
cases.summary: The applicant, Dato' Seri Timor Shah Rafiq, had earlier obtained leave from the High Court to commence a statutory derivative action in the name of and on behalf of Nautilus Tug & Towage Sdn. Bhd. — the mechanism by which a shareholder or director may sue on a company's behalf when the company itself will not act. That leave order was granted and then perfected (formally sealed and entered). After the leave order was perfected, the applicant's office as a director of the company was vacated. The company then applied to set aside the leave order, arguing in substance that the loss of office undermined or invalidated the leave that had been given. The court's published catchwords frame the issues as: whether the court was functus officio (that is, whether it had already exhausted its authority over the matter once the leave order was perfected, so that it could not revisit its own order); whether the applicant's subsequent loss of directorship operated retrospectively to invalidate the leave order; and whether any of the recognised exceptions permitting a court to set aside or vary a perfected order had been made out. The court held that none of the recognised exceptions were established and dismissed the setting-aside application, leaving the leave order intact.
cases.keyPoint: Once an order granting leave to bring a statutory derivative action has been perfected, the court is generally functus officio, and a change in the applicant's status (such as later ceasing to be a director) does not retrospectively invalidate that leave unless a recognised exception to the finality of perfected orders applies.
cases.plain: A company director got the court's permission to sue on behalf of his company — something you need special permission for, because normally only the company can bring its own lawsuits. After that permission was formally issued, he stopped being a director. The company went back to the judge and said the permission should be cancelled because he no longer held that post. The judge said no: once a court order has been properly issued and sealed, the same court can't simply undo it except in a few narrow situations, and losing the directorship later doesn't reach back in time to cancel permission that was validly granted. So the permission stands and the case can go on.

cases.title: Ng Yin Ping v Derek Kwok Kee Yeung & Anor (Kang Cheow Sean, Party Cited)
cases.court: High Court of Malaya at Penang (Mahkamah Tinggi) — divorce and matrimonial proceedings
cases.dateRaw: 10 November 2026 (grounds of judgment uploaded to the e-Judgment portal on 13 November 2026)
cases.outcome: The judgment deals with the Party Cited's application (Enclosure 19) to be struck out or removed from the husband's Answer and Cross-Petition. The portal listing available to me sets out the facts and the issue but does not state the final disposal, and I will not guess at it — the PDF grounds on the e-Judgment portal should be read for the order made.
cases.summary: This is a divorce proceeding begun by the wife, Ng Yin Ping, against the husband, Derek Kwok Kee Yeung, in which she seeks various reliefs arising from the breakdown of the marriage. The wife named a woman, Olga Marianne Rostaqui ep. Petithomme, as Co-Respondent on allegations that the husband had committed adultery with her. The husband filed an Answer and Cross-Petition dated 26 November 2025, in which he in turn named Kang Cheow Sean as a 'Party Cited', alleging that the Party Cited was involved in an adulterous relationship with the wife, and seeking, among other things, an order that the Party Cited pay him damages for adultery. The judgment concerns the Party Cited's own application, in Enclosure 19, to be struck out and/or removed as a party to the husband's Answer and Cross-Petition. That application was brought under Order 18 rule 19 and Order 92 rule 4 of the Rules of Court 2012, read with rule 103 of the Divorce and Matrimonial Proceedings Rules 1980. The question the court identified for determination was whether, on these facts, the Party Cited should be removed on the basis that the pleadings disclose no reasonable cause of action against him, and/or that naming him was scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of the court's process.
cases.keyPoint: A person named as a 'Party Cited' in a cross-petition alleging adultery may apply to be struck out where the pleadings disclose no reasonable cause of action against him or where his joinder is scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process, under O.18 r.19 and O.92 r.4 of the Rules of Court 2012 read with rule 103 of the Divorce and Matrimonial Proceedings Rules 1980.
cases.plain: A wife asked the court for a divorce and accused her husband of having an affair, naming the other woman in her petition. The husband fought back with his own cross-claim, accusing the wife of having an affair too, and dragged the man he said she was involved with into the case — asking the court to make that man pay him compensation. That man then asked to be taken out of the case entirely, saying there was no proper legal claim against him and that naming him was just harassment. This judgment is the court dealing with that request to be removed from the divorce proceedings. The published court listing explains the background and the question the judge had to answer, but does not show what the judge finally ordered, so the full written grounds on the e-Judgment portal need to be read for the result.
